name: Thymosin alpha-1
used_for: A 28-amino-acid peptide (thymalfasin, brand Zadaxin) studied mainly in China, Europe and elsewhere for chronic hepatitis B, sepsis and COVID-19, and promoted online for immune support. No FDA-approved product was found (no Drugs@FDA or DailyMed entry for thymalfasin or thymosin). FDA's compounding page lists thymosin-alpha-1 among bulk substances nominated for compounding that were previously in category 2 (potential safety concerns) and later withdrawn by the nominators. Trial results are mixed: some hepatitis B and sepsis trials were modestly positive or borderline, and other work found no benefit.

entries.text: 0.8 mg or 1.6 mg of thymosin alpha-1 monotherapy for 24 weeks, with follow-up to 72 weeks; similar response rates in both groups (for example 22.8% HBe-antigen clearance at 1.6 mg).
entries.population: 316 Japanese adults with chronic hepatitis B

entries.text: 1.6 mg subcutaneously once daily for 1 week added to standard care (registered phase 2 trial, terminated early with 56 enrolled, no results posted).
entries.population: Hospitalized adults with COVID-19 and lymphocytopenia

administration_guidance.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says thymosin alpha-1 has no specified time of day, with the emphasis on consistent spacing between injections. It says the abdomen, thigh or upper arm are used with rotation, and that a mixed vial is kept at 2 to 8 C and used within about 30 days without freezing.
administration_guidance.label: internet

administration_guidance.text: Another educational protocol wiki that lists supplier links says a reconstituted thymosin alpha-1 vial should be used immediately and any remainder discarded, because the preparation has no preservative. This conflicts with the 30-day figure given elsewhere.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: In a randomized trial of thymosin alpha-1 in 316 Japanese patients with chronic hepatitis B, adverse drug reactions were mild and mostly involved fluctuations in liver enzymes.
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: In a randomized trial of 361 ICU patients with severe sepsis, no serious drug-related adverse event was recorded.
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says reactions to thymosin alpha-1 are usually mild, mainly redness, soreness or swelling at the injection site that resolves within hours, transient fatigue early on, and flu-like symptoms.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: A health-information site describes thymosin alpha-1 as helping autoimmune disease, cancers, hepatitis, COVID-19, ME/CFS and sepsis, and says Zadaxin is FDA-approved; FDA sources found for this review show no US approval, so the claim conflicts with them.

A physician's practice page says thymosin alpha-1 may strengthen and balance the immune system, rebalance autoimmune conditions such as Hashimoto's, and improve sepsis survival, and promotes booking a call for local patients; it notes it is not FDA-approved for general use.

research.summary: FDA page on bulk drug substances for compounding that may present significant safety risks (content current as of 04/22/2026).
research.finding: Under the heading of substances nominated but withdrawn, it lists thymosin-alpha-1 and says compounded drugs may pose a significant risk of immunogenicity for certain routes and have peptide impurity and characterization complexities, and that the safety information is inadequate. It does not say the substance is approved.

research.summary: ETASS: multicenter, single-blind randomized trial of thymosin alpha-1 plus standard care versus standard care alone in 361 ICU patients with severe sepsis in China (Wu et al., Crit Care; NCT00711620).
research.finding: 28-day mortality was 26.0% with thymosin versus 35.0% in controls, a borderline result (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.02). Immune marker mHLA-DR improved more. Patients and standard care were not placebo-blinded.

research.summary: Randomized comparison of thymosin alpha-1 0.8 mg versus 1.6 mg for 24 weeks in 316 Japanese patients with chronic hepatitis B (Iino et al., J Viral Hepat).
research.finding: Both doses produced similar response rates (about 22.8% HBe-antigen clearance and 36.4% ALT normalization at 1.6 mg at 72 weeks); adverse reactions were mild. There was no placebo group, so benefit versus no treatment is not shown.

research.summary: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial adding thymosin alpha-1 to interferon versus interferon alone in 98 people with HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (Lim et al., Antivir Ther).
research.finding: HBeAg loss was 45.8% with the combination and 28.0% with interferon alone, a difference that did not reach statistical significance (p=0.067); no significant differences were found for other endpoints.

research.summary: Phase 2 open-label trial of thymalfasin versus no extra treatment in hospitalized adults with COVID-19 and lymphocytopenia (56 enrolled; ClinicalTrials.gov).
research.finding: The study was terminated early because of slow enrollment and the principal investigator moving institutions; no results are posted, so it provides no efficacy data.
